text: Chapter 1 — Arjuna Vishada Yoga (The Yoga of Arjuna's Despair). On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna sees his kinsmen, teachers, and friends arrayed for war on both sides. Overcome by grief and compassion, he drops his bow Gandiva, refuses to fight, and asks Krishna for guidance. This chapter sets the stage for the entire Gita: a soul paralyzed by doubt, attachment, and moral confusion turns to the Divine for clarity.

Chapter 2 — Sankhya Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge). Krishna begins his teaching. He explains that the soul (atman) is eternal, indestructible, and untouched by birth or death; only the body perishes. He introduces karma-yoga: act according to your duty (svadharma) without attachment to the fruits of action. He describes the sthitaprajna — the person of steady wisdom who is unshaken by pleasure or pain, gain or loss, praise or blame.

Chapter 3 — Karma Yoga (The Yoga of Action). Krishna explains that no one can remain even for a moment without acting. Renouncing action is impossible; what must be renounced is attachment to the fruits of action. Selfless action, performed as yajna (sacrifice) without ego, purifies the heart and leads to liberation. Krishna distinguishes desire (kama) and anger as the great enemies of the self, born of rajas, the passionate quality.

Chapter 4 — Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge and Renunciation of Action). Krishna reveals that this eternal yoga was first taught to Vivasvan, the sun-god, and passed down through a lineage of sages. He explains his own divine incarnations (avataras): 'Whenever there is decline of dharma and rise of adharma, I manifest myself.' Knowledge, he says, is the supreme purifier — the fire of wisdom reduces all karma to ashes.

Chapter 5 — Karma Sanyasa Yoga (The Yoga of Renunciation of Action). Krishna reconciles the two paths — action (karma-yoga) and renunciation (sanyasa). Both lead to the same goal, but karma-yoga, action without attachment, is easier and surer. The truly wise see the same Self in a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. Such a one, established in Brahman, is freed from duality and rests in inner peace.

Chapter 6 — Dhyana Yoga (The Yoga of Meditation). Krishna teaches the practice of meditation in detail: posture, place, moderation in eating, sleeping, and activity. The mind, restless as the wind, must be tamed through steady practice (abhyasa) and dispassion (vairagya). Arjuna doubts whether such a practice is possible; Krishna assures him that no sincere effort on this path is ever lost — the yogi continues from where he left off in a future life.

Chapter 7 — Jnana Vijnana Yoga (The Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom). Krishna reveals his two natures: the lower prakriti made of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego; and the higher prakriti, the conscious life-principle that sustains the universe. Of those who worship, he names four kinds: the distressed, the seeker of wealth, the curious, and the wise — and among them, the wise devotee is dearest to him.

Chapter 8 — Akshara Brahma Yoga (The Yoga of the Imperishable Brahman). Krishna explains the nature of Brahman, the Self (adhyatma), action (karma), and the supreme spirit. The moment of death is decisive: 'Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body, that state one attains.' He describes the bright and dark paths after death — the path of return and the path of no-return — and urges remembrance of the Divine at all times.

Chapter 9 — Raja Vidya Raja Guhya Yoga (The Yoga of Royal Knowledge and Royal Secret). Krishna calls this the king of sciences, the king of secrets, the supreme purifier. The whole universe is pervaded by him in his unmanifest form; all beings rest in him, yet he is not in them. He promises: 'Whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water with devotion — that I accept.' Surrender, however small in form, is met with infinite grace.

Chapter 10 — Vibhuti Yoga (The Yoga of Divine Glories). Arjuna asks how he should contemplate the Divine. Krishna lists his vibhutis — his most splendid manifestations in the world: among the Adityas he is Vishnu, among lights the radiant sun, among the Vedas the Sama Veda, among rivers the Ganges, among warriors Rama, among trees the Ashvattha, and 'whatever is glorious, beautiful, or mighty — know that to be a spark of my splendor.'

Chapter 11 — Vishvarupa Darshana Yoga (The Yoga of the Vision of the Cosmic Form). Arjuna asks to see Krishna's universal form. Granted divine sight, he beholds the Vishvarupa — all gods, all worlds, all beings, all time arising and dissolving within Krishna's body — a vision both glorious and terrifying. Arjuna trembles and prays for forgiveness for past familiarities. Krishna assures him: this form is rare even for the gods; only loving devotion (bhakti) can reveal it.

Chapter 12 — Bhakti Yoga (The Yoga of Devotion). Asked whether worship of the personal form or the unmanifest Absolute is better, Krishna answers that both reach him, but the path of devotion to the personal form is easier for embodied beings. He describes the qualities of his beloved devotee: free from hatred, friendly and compassionate, without ego or possessiveness, equal in pain and pleasure, content, self-controlled, and firmly devoted with mind and intellect fixed in him.

Chapter 13 — Kshetra Kshetrajna Vibhaga Yoga (The Yoga of the Field and the Knower of the Field). Krishna distinguishes the kshetra (the body, the field) from the kshetrajna (the Self, the knower of the field). True knowledge is humility, non-injury, forbearance, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-control, and constant equanimity. The Self is one in all beings; he who sees this sees rightly. Prakriti acts; Purusha witnesses.

Chapter 14 — Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga (The Yoga of the Three Gunas). Krishna describes the three qualities of nature: sattva (purity, light, harmony), rajas (passion, restlessness, craving), and tamas (inertia, dullness, delusion). All beings are bound by these. The wise one observes them as the actors and is not their slave. By unwavering devotion, one rises beyond the three gunas and is fit for union with Brahman.

Chapter 15 — Purushottama Yoga (The Yoga of the Supreme Self). Krishna describes the cosmic Ashvattha tree, whose roots are above and branches below, sustained by the gunas. The wise cut this tree with the axe of non-attachment and reach the eternal abode. He distinguishes the perishable (kshara), the imperishable (akshara), and the Purushottama — the Supreme Person who transcends both and pervades all worlds.

Chapter 16 — Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga (The Yoga of the Divine and Demoniacal Natures). Krishna contrasts two kinds of human disposition. The divine nature is marked by fearlessness, purity, charity, self-restraint, study, austerity, straightforwardness, non-violence, truth, absence of anger, compassion, gentleness, modesty, steadiness. The demoniacal is marked by hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance. Three gates of hell — lust, anger, and greed — must be abandoned.

Chapter 17 — Shraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga (The Yoga of the Threefold Faith). Faith is of three kinds, shaped by the dominant guna. Krishna classifies food, sacrifice, austerity, and charity into sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic varieties. He explains the sacred syllable Aum Tat Sat as designating Brahman — chanted at the start, middle, and completion of every worthy action. Whatever is done without faith is called asat, unreal, and bears no fruit here or hereafter.

Chapter 18 — Moksha Sanyasa Yoga (The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation). The longest chapter, summarizing the whole Gita. Krishna distinguishes sannyasa (renunciation of action) from tyaga (renunciation of the fruits of action) and praises the latter. He explains how knowledge, action, and the doer fall under the three gunas. Finally he gives his most intimate teaching: 'Abandon all dharmas and take refuge in me alone; I shall liberate you from all sins — do not grieve.' Arjuna's doubts are dispelled; he is ready to act.
